title: Jivaka and meat
hookLine: the physician asks about meat; the monks' rule: not if seen, heard or suspected killed for them

lines: NEVER. IT DEPENDS. WHATEVER IS OFFERED.
cards: Do Buddhists eat meat? Ask around and you may hear three answers. Never.
It depends. Whatever is offered. Each answer has its own teachers and texts behind it.

The question is old. Jivaka, a physician who, tradition says, cared for a king and for the Buddha himself, once heard a rumor about the Buddha's food. Instead of repeating it, he went straight to the source to ask.

teach.b: This is the fifty-fifth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse to Jivaka. Jivaka says: I've heard people say that living beings are killed for the Buddha, and he knowingly eats meat prepared for him.
Is that true? Those who say that, the Buddha answers, misrepresent me. Then he gives the rule.

teach.h: NOT IF SEEN, HEARD OR SUSPECTED
teach.b: There are three cases in which meat should not be eaten by a monk: when it's seen, heard or suspected that the animal was killed for him. Otherwise, a monk who lives on alms eats what is put in his bowl, without choosing.
A monk who lives with loving-kindness eats without greed, without infatuation, seeing the danger in food and the escape from it.
And anyone who kills a living being for the Buddha or his disciples makes much demerit: in ordering it, in the animal being dragged, in the killing, in the pain, and in offering what isn't allowable.
Buddhists today live this question in different ways, and each has reasons. Theravada monks keep this three-part rule and accept what lay people offer.
In Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese monasteries the custom is vegetarian, drawing on later Mahayana sutras that teach against eating meat out of compassion.
In Tibetan communities practice varies, and some teachers encourage vegetarianism where it's possible. Underneath all of them sits the line Jivaka heard: no animal is to be killed for the monk.
Every meal has a story behind it.

how: Theravada monastics follow the threefold rule from MN 55 and the Vinaya, accepting what is offered; Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese monastics keep a vegetarian diet, as do some lay Buddhists; in Tibetan communities practice varies, and some teachers encourage vegetarianism.

o: a physician who asked the Buddha directly
a monk who never ate any meat
a king who fed the monks every day

p: the three cases: don't eat it
eats what's put in the bowl
killing an animal for the Buddha

s: all Buddhists follow the same rule about meat
Theravada monks follow MN 55's threefold rule; Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese monasteries keep a vegetarian custom; Tibetan practice varies.
the Buddha said those spreading the rumor misrepresented him
he denied knowingly eating meat killed for him, and gave the threefold rule.
in MN 55 a monk chooses what food he receives
a monk on alms round eats what is put in his bowl, without choosing, except in the three cases.

games.q: you're a monk on alms round. a householder offers you a meat dish, and you overhear that the animal was killed this morning especially for you. what does the rule say?
o: accept it; you didn't kill it.
don't eat it: it was heard to be killed for you.
games.why: heard that it was killed for you: that's one of the three cases. the monk should not eat it.

practice: Picture the last meal you ate and follow one ingredient back: the store, the truck, the farm, the field or the animal, the hands that grew it, cut it, carried it.
Don't judge; just see how many lives touched it, and let some gratitude come for all of it. Then think of your next meal, and what eating it with care might look like.

wordCard.voice: Jivaka. The physician's question, and the monks' threefold rule: not if seen, heard or suspected killed for them.

carryVoice: Your line: know your food. Every bowl has hands and lives behind it. Day four hundred forty-seven.
